scenarios.scenario: Company policy says the assistant must never modify files under secrets/ or run shell commands that touch them, even when a crafted prompt or its own reasoning argues otherwise. Compliance wants a guarantee, not a convention it usually follows.

key.primary: PreToolUse hook (type: command) matched on Edit|Write and Bash that inspects tool input and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: deny, configured in settings.json
key.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule stating 'never touch files under secrets/'
key.rejection_reason: The memory docs are explicit that CLAUDE.md and auto memory are context, not enforced configuration: 'To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead.' Hooks are evaluated by the client before the tool call executes, so the deny happens regardless of what the model decided; a memory instruction depends entirely on model compliance.
key.lifecycle: Fires on the PreToolUse event before every matching tool call; deny reason is fed back to the model
key.failure_mode: With only a CLAUDE.md rule, long-context drift or a prompt injection eventually produces one edit to secrets/ and nothing in the pipeline stops it; adherence degrades further as CLAUDE.md grows

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook registered in managed policy settings, matching Edit|Write|Bash (and the PowerShell tool), that inspects tool_input and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision "deny" (or exits 2) for any path or command string touching secrets/. Back it with permissions.deny rules such as Edit(./secrets/**), Read(./secrets/**) and Bash deny patterns, since deny rules are evaluated by the harness in every permission mode including bypassPermissions and auto mode.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule (or a stated conversational boundary) telling Claude never to touch secrets/ - the docs are explicit that a conversational boundary is re-read from the transcript and can be lost to compaction, so it is not the hard guarantee compliance is asking for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Both the permission-rule evaluator and the PreToolUse hook run outside the model's control loop; the model never sees a choice, the tool call is refused before execution and only the denial reason is returned to it.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook executes in its own OS process with the tool-call JSON on stdin, so the matching logic never occupies the session context window. Only the short permissionDecisionReason string crosses back into the conversation, which is also what the model would use to reason about a workaround.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, from the first tool use until the session ends; it applies regardless of permission mode and cannot be switched off mid-session. Placing it in managed policy settings with allowManagedHooksOnly stops a developer removing it from user or project settings.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on the tool call, but the Bash surface is the weak spot: prefix-style deny patterns are trivially evaded by indirection (variables, command substitution, symlinks, a helper script), so the hook must normalise and inspect the actual command text rather than trust a glob. If the hook script itself errors with a code other than 2 the call is treated as a non-blocking error and execution continues, so the script must default to deny on parse failure.
sheets.version_caveat: Only exit code 2 blocks; exit 1 is non-blocking. Hooks run without a controlling terminal as of v2.1.139, so they cannot write to /dev/tty. Managed policy settings with allowManagedHooksOnly (and permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode) are the enterprise-plan controls that make this non-overridable; deny and ask rules apply in every mode, while allow rules are the ones dropped under bypassPermissions.

sheets.primary: Hook: a PreToolUse handler matched on Write, Edit and Bash that inspects tool_input (file_path, or the command string for Bash) and returns permissionDecision deny for anything resolving under secrets/, shipped in a managed-policy settings file and paired with permissions.deny rules for the same paths. The decision axis that settled it is the first one, who owns enforcement: this is a checkable invariant, not judgment that varies by context, so the harness must own the firing.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A rule in CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules stating that secrets/ is off limits.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Hooks run on the lifecycle event regardless of what the model concludes, and on PreToolUse an exit code 2 blocks the tool call outright, so a crafted prompt cannot argue the guard out of firing. CLAUDE.md by contrast is context the model may weigh against other instructions.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler runs as a separate process outside the model's context window. It receives one JSON object on stdin (hook_event_name, tool_name, tool_input, cwd, session_id) and the only thing that crosses back into the conversation is the block decision plus its reason string, so the policy logic itself never enters context and cannot be reasoned about or rewritten by the model.
sheets.lifecycle: It fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, in every session where those settings load, and it keeps applying until the entry is removed from the settings file. It has no notion of task completion, so it also blocks the legitimate case until someone changes the policy.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed only if you write it that way. A command handler that crashes or times out exits with a code other than 0 or 2, which is a non-blocking error, and the tool proceeds; an http handler has no exit-2 equivalent at all and fails open on connection failure or timeout. The other real failure is a coverage gap: a matcher that misses a tool or a Bash form that reaches the path indirectly is a silent false negative, and from the outside a crash and a deliberate block look identical.
sheets.version_caveat: The guarantee compliance wants exists only at the managed tier: disableAllHooks set in user, project or local settings cannot disable managed hooks, and only disableAllHooks at the managed settings level can. Ship the hook and the deny rules through managed policy settings, and confirm the PreToolUse event and the handler type exist on the installed build.

sheets.primary: A harness-enforced permission layer: `permissions.deny` rules in managed policy settings covering the path (Read/Edit/Write on the secrets tree) plus a `PreToolUse` hook matching Write|Edit|Bash that inspects the tool input and returns `permissionDecision: "deny"` (or exits 2) when it resolves to secrets/. Step 1 put the hook first; step 2 changed the ordering, because the docs name the permission system as the authoritative mechanism for hard allows and denies and say hooks cannot override it, so the deny rules are the guarantee and the hook is the programmatic complement that can read an arbitrary Bash command string.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule (or a `.claude/rules/` entry) saying never touch secrets/. It loses because CLAUDE.md is delivered as context, not enforced configuration, with no guarantee of compliance, which is exactly the convention compliance says is insufficient.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Settings rules are enforced by the client regardless of what Claude decides to do, and CLAUDE.md instructions shape behavior but are not a hard enforcement layer; the model never gets a vote once a deny rule or a deny-returning PreToolUse hook matches.
sheets.context_boundary: Neither layer runs in the model's context window: the hook is a separate process receiving the tool call as JSON on stdin, and the deny rules are evaluated by the client. The only thing that crosses back in is the short denial reason string (stderr on exit 2, or `permissionDecisionReason`).
sheets.lifecycle: The deny rules apply for every tool call from settings load onward, machine-wide when deployed as managed policy; the PreToolUse hook fires before every matching tool call and stops when the session ends. Hooks from all settings levels merge rather than replace each other, so the managed rule cannot be removed by a project or user file.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for anything the rule or matcher actually matches, and fails open for anything it does not: a Bash invocation that reaches the path by a form the pattern does not cover slips through. The hook mechanics are the sharp edge, exit code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error and execution continues, only exit code 2 (or an explicit deny) blocks, and a timed-out hook lets the call proceed, which is why the permission deny rules and not the hook carry the guarantee.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on either mechanism, but administrators can set `allowManagedHooksOnly` to block user and project hooks (exempting certain plugins), and only managed policy settings are non-overridable by the user; a hook declared in project settings is also subject to the workspace trust gate.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook configured in settings.json, matching the file-editing tools (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit) and Bash, that inspects the tool input and returns a deny decision for any path or command string resolving under secrets/. Pair it with a permissions deny list in settings.json so the harness refuses the call even before the hook runs. Because the harness evaluates it, no amount of prompt argument or model reasoning can talk past it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A rule written into CLAUDE.md (or a project rules file) telling the assistant never to touch secrets/. Rejected because CLAUDE.md is an instruction the model may reweigh under pressure or forget in a long context, which is exactly the convention compliance says is not good enough.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook process, not the model, produces the allow or deny verdict, and the harness aborts the tool call on a block regardless of what the model intended.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs as a separate OS process outside any model context window; it receives the tool name and tool input as JSON on stdin. Only the block decision and its short reason string cross back into the main session context, so the model sees a refusal message rather than the hook's logic.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call, before execution, for as long as the settings file declaring it is in scope (user, project, or managed policy settings). It stops applying only if the settings entry is removed or the matcher stops matching; it is not session-scoped and does not expire mid-conversation.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails closed for the calls it actually matches, but the realistic failure is coverage rather than bypass: a Bash command can reach the same bytes through a symlink, a relative path, a variable, a heredoc, a python -c one-liner, or a tool the matcher does not list, and a naive substring check on 'secrets/' will miss all of those. If the hook script itself crashes or times out the behaviour depends on how the harness treats a non-blocking exit status, which is where a silent fail-open can creep in, so the script should deny on its own internal errors.
sheets.version_caveat: I do not know the exact Claude Code version that introduced the structured JSON hook output with an explicit permission decision field, nor the current exact field names, so the hook should be written and then live-tested against the installed version. The convention I am confident about is that a non-zero blocking exit status from PreToolUse stops the call; the richer JSON schema and the settings.json permissions deny syntax have both changed across releases and I cannot name the versions.

scenarios.scenario: Our release runbook is about 400 lines of ordered steps plus two helper scripts. It is needed roughly once a week, and the team resents that every conversation pays a token cost for it even during unrelated work.

key.primary: An Agent Skill: a .claude/skills/release-runbook/SKILL.md with a description, the procedure in the body, and the scripts as supporting files
key.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in the project CLAUDE.md (or an @-import from it)
key.rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md and its imports load in full at the start of every session; the skills doc says to create a skill 'when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact' because 'a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.' Only the skill's description sits in context until invocation.
key.lifecycle: Description is always listed to the model; full body loads when the model matches it to the task or the user types /release-runbook
key.failure_mode: As CLAUDE.md, the 400 lines consume context in every session; the memory docs warn files over ~200 lines reduce adherence, so both the runbook and the rest of CLAUDE.md get followed less reliably

sheets.primary: Skill: .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md holding the ordered steps, with the two helper scripts and any bulk reference material as sibling files that load only when the body points at them. This is the axis of procedural knowledge versus always-on fact, and a weekly procedure is exactly the case the skill body's on-demand loading exists for.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md (or an @path import into it), which is what the team is paying for today.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. A skill is instruction text Claude reads and then follows; nothing in the harness checks that step 7 actually ran, so the release discipline remains the model's to keep.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context, but only on demand. Before invocation the session carries the skill's name and description for discovery; the body enters as one message when Claude matches the description or a user types /release, and supporting files cross the boundary only when the body references them.
sheets.lifecycle: It loads on a description match or an explicit /release, and the rendered body then stays in the session and is not re-read, so it should be written as standing instructions rather than one-time steps. It stops applying at the end of the session, and compaction re-attaches only a truncated copy, so load-bearing rules belong early in the file.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, and it fails open in two directions. Discovery failure is the common one: a vague description means the skill never fires, the release runs from memory, and nobody notices because the outcome still looks plausible. The second is self-inflicted: pasting all 400 lines into SKILL.md re-imports the token cost you moved out of CLAUDE.md, because it is the body, not the reference files, that loads on use.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on the mechanism itself, but note the migration: custom commands were merged into skills, so a legacy .claude/commands/release.md produces the same /release and is documented as the legacy format with .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md as the recommended one. Do not leave both in place, or /release is ambiguous.

sheets.primary: A skill: a directory containing SKILL.md whose YAML frontmatter carries only a name and a description, with the 400 lines of ordered steps in the body and the two helper scripts as sibling files the skill tells the assistant to execute rather than read. Progressive disclosure is the whole point here: only the short description is resident at session start, and the body is pulled into context on the week the release actually happens.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md. Rejected precisely because CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session's context unconditionally, which is the token cost the team is complaining about.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness makes the skill available and reads its metadata, but the decision to load and follow it comes from the model matching the description to the current task.
sheets.context_boundary: At startup only the skill's name and description occupy the main context. On invocation the SKILL.md body is read into that same main session context; the helper scripts ideally never enter context at all, since they are run as subprocesses and only their output crosses back.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered when the model judges the task matches the description, or when a user names it explicitly. Once loaded it stays resident for the remainder of that context window, so it stops applying on a clear, a compaction that drops it, or a new session.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open in the discovery direction: if the description is vague the model simply never loads it and improvises the release from memory, which is worse than a missing runbook because it looks like compliance. The opposite failure is over-triggering on unrelated work, which reintroduces the token cost the team wanted removed. Neither failure is visible unless someone checks whether the skill was actually invoked.
sheets.version_caveat: Skills as a first-class Claude Code mechanism arrived relatively late and were beta before being broadly available; I do not know the exact minimum version, and I am not certain whether an allowed-tools style frontmatter key is supported in the installed release. If the installed version predates skills, the fallback is a slash command file, which is user-invoked but also not always resident.

sheets.primary: A project skill at .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md, with the 400 ordered steps split into on-demand reference files in the skill directory and the two helper scripts shipped alongside and invoked by path rather than pasted inline. Only the skill's name and description sit in context at startup; the body loads when Claude invokes it or the operator types /release.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md - CLAUDE.md content is injected as a user message on every session regardless of relevance, which is exactly the per-conversation token cost the team is objecting to.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness only surfaces the skill's metadata and loads the body on request; whether the runbook is followed, and followed in order, is the model's decision.
sheets.context_boundary: Runs in the main session context. At startup only the frontmatter description crosses in; the SKILL.md body crosses in when triggered, and each reference file only when the model reads it. Helper scripts run as subprocesses, so only their stdout enters context, not their source.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered by the model matching the description to the task, or by the human typing /release; it stops applying when the release conversation ends. It is reloaded per session from disk, so edits take effect on the next session with no install step.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. The usual failures are a vague description so the model never loads the skill (the runbook silently does not happen), and step-skipping or reordering on a 400-line procedure once it is loaded. Enforce the irreversible steps with hooks or permission rules rather than trusting the prose.
sheets.version_caveat: Custom commands were merged into skills, so an existing .claude/commands/release.md still works and produces the same /release, but only the skills/ directory layout gives you the supporting-file directory and the invocation-control frontmatter. Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, with Claude-Code-only extensions such as subagent execution and dynamic context injection.

sheets.primary: A skill at `.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md` holding the ordered runbook, with the two helper scripts as supporting files in the same skill directory and referenced from the body. Only the name and description sit in context at session start; the 400 lines load when someone types `/release` or Claude matches the description.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md. It loses on exactly the complaint raised: CLAUDE.md loads its full content at session start and is re-billed on every request, whether or not the week's work is a release.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. A skill is instructions Claude reads and follows, so the outcome varies with Claude's interpretation, unlike a hook whose trigger is guaranteed.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context window. Descriptions cross the boundary at session start; the full body and any referenced files cross only on invocation, and once loaded they stay in the conversation for the rest of the session.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads on demand, when the user invokes `/release` or Claude matches the task to the skill description, and never loads on the unrelated weeks. It stops applying when the session ends or the context is cleared.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory. The documented failure is description matching: if descriptions are vague or overlap with other skills, Claude may load the wrong skill or miss one that would have helped, and a 400-step procedure invites partial execution. Invoking `/release` explicitly is the documented way to force the right one.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate or plan restriction is documented for skills. The relevant knob is `disable-model-invocation: true` in the frontmatter, which hides the skill from Claude entirely and drops its context cost to zero until manually invoked, or `skillOverrides` in settings to do the same to a skill you did not author.

scenarios.scenario: During coding sessions the assistant should look up and update tickets in our self-hosted tracker, which sits behind OAuth. Copy-pasting ticket text into the chat is exactly what we are trying to eliminate.

key.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added via claude mcp add / .mcp.json, exposing query and update tools with OAuth handled by the MCP authentication flow
key.rejected_alternative: A skill whose SKILL.md instructs Claude to call the tracker's REST API with bundled curl scripts
key.rejection_reason: The MCP docs describe exactly this trigger: 'Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker.' MCP gives typed tools, a managed OAuth flow, and per-tool permissioning; a script-based skill leaves credential storage, token refresh, and response parsing as hand-rolled shell plumbing.
key.lifecycle: Server connects at session start per its configured scope; the model calls its tools during turns subject to permission rules
key.failure_mode: The curl-skill version breaks on token expiry, requires secrets exposed to the shell environment, and every invocation is an unvetted Bash call rather than a scoped, individually permissionable tool

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added with the HTTP transport (claude mcp add --transport http tracker https://tracker.internal/mcp) at project scope so the entry lives in the repo's .mcp.json, with each developer completing the browser OAuth flow once via /mcp then selecting Authenticate.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that shells out to the tracker's REST API with curl - it would work, but it pushes token storage, refresh and OAuth callback handling into a script instead of using the transport layer that already handles them.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the connection, the OAuth handshake and token storage, and gates the first tool call behind a permission prompt. The model owns when to call a tool and what to write back into a ticket.
sheets.context_boundary: Runs in the main session context, but the server's tool schemas and server instructions are loaded into every session's context window whether used or not. Across the boundary go the tool arguments the model emits and the JSON results the server returns; the OAuth token never enters context.
sheets.lifecycle: Connects at session start when Claude Code reads .mcp.json, and each new teammate gets a one-time approval prompt for the project-scoped server. It stops at session end; the OAuth grant persists until it expires or is revoked, at which point the server reverts to "Needs authentication".
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed and loudly: an expired grant or unreachable host shows "Needs authentication" or "Failed to connect" and the tools simply are not offered, so Claude falls back to asking the human, which is the pasting behaviour you were removing. The quieter cost is context: a chatty tracker server's tool definitions consume window on every turn.
sheets.version_caveat: .mcp.json is read once at session start, so edits need a restart, and a previously rejected server needs claude mcp reset-project-choices. Startup times out at 30s unless MCP_TIMEOUT is raised. From v2.1.191 a 404 names the URL it tried. Consider MCP tool search to defer tool definitions, and managed MCP policy settings if the org needs to allowlist servers.

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added over HTTP transport (`claude mcp add --transport http tracker https://...`) and authenticated with the browser OAuth flow from `/mcp` then Authenticate. Register it at project scope so the entry lives in a committed `.mcp.json` and every engineer on the repo gets the same tools.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill wrapping a `curl` or CLI script against the tracker API. It loses because the skill would have to carry token handling itself and gives Claude prose instructions rather than typed tools, whereas the MCP server owns the connection and authentication.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, with the harness owning the plumbing: Claude Code manages the connection, the OAuth sign-in, and which tools are exposed, and it prompts for permission the first time a server tool is called. The model owns only the decision of when to call a tool and what to do with the result.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context. Tool names from connected servers load at session start with full JSON schemas deferred until a tool is needed, and tool results come back into the main conversation. Each connected server costs some context because its tool names and server instructions load into every session.
sheets.lifecycle: Servers connect at session start once configured; `.mcp.json` is read at session start, so edits need a session restart. A project-scoped server shows `Pending approval` until each teammate approves it once, and the OAuth session persists until the token is revoked or expires, after which `/mcp` shows `Needs authentication`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed in the useful sense: an unauthenticated or unreachable server shows `Needs authentication`, `Failed to connect`, or `Connection error` and its tools are simply unavailable rather than silently wrong. The practical traps are the 30-second startup timeout (raise with `MCP_TIMEOUT`), a rejected project approval that needs `claude mcp reset-project-choices`, and the fact that a self-hosted server's responses are third-party text entering the model's context.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan restriction, but project-scoped servers are gated behind a per-user approval prompt by design, and error reporting is version dependent: as of v2.1.191 an HTTP server returning 404 reports `MCP endpoint not found at <url>`, while earlier versions show a generic `Error POSTing to endpoint` without the URL.

sheets.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, configured for the project in .mcp.json, exposing get-ticket, search-tickets and update-ticket style tools. If the tracker offers a remote MCP endpoint, use the HTTP or SSE transport with its OAuth flow so the harness holds the token; otherwise write a small local stdio server that performs the OAuth exchange and stores the refresh token outside the repo.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that wraps curl calls to the tracker API. Rejected because it makes every call a shell invocation with a token the model can see and echo, gives no structured tool schema, and puts credential handling in a place the harness cannot manage or revoke.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, but primarily the harness for the connection: the harness owns transport, the OAuth handshake, token storage and the per-tool permission prompts. The model owns the judgment of when to look up or update a ticket, and that part is not enforceable.
sheets.context_boundary: The server is a separate process or remote service with its own memory; nothing of its internals enters the session. What crosses into the main context is the tool schemas at connection time (a fixed per-session token cost proportional to how many tools the server exposes) and each tool result payload, which is why the server should return trimmed ticket fields rather than raw API JSON.
sheets.lifecycle: Connected when a session starts in a directory whose config lists it, and it lives for the session; project-scoped .mcp.json entries typically require a one-time user approval per project before they will load. It stops applying when the session ends, when the server process dies, or when the OAuth token expires and is not refreshed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly: an expired or revoked token, or a server that failed to start, usually surfaces as the tools simply not being there, and the model then falls back to asking the human to paste ticket text, which is the exact behaviour being eliminated. Secondary failures are context bloat when the server exposes dozens of tools, and write amplification, since an update-ticket tool lets the model mutate the tracker on its own judgment unless the permission config forces a prompt on the write tools.
sheets.version_caveat: OAuth support for remote MCP servers, and the project-scoped .mcp.json approval flow, both came in later Claude Code releases and I cannot name the exact versions. Self-hosted trackers behind a private network may also need the server to run locally rather than as a remote endpoint, and I do not know whether the installed release supports every transport variant.

sheets.primary: MCP server: register the tracker over the http transport (claude mcp add --transport http tracker <url>) at project scope so the entry lands in a committed .mcp.json, and let each developer complete the browser sign-in through /mcp once. The axis is the one about external data behind an authenticated boundary, which is what MCP exists for and what a shell wrapper cannot give you.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Skill that wraps curl or the tracker's CLI, carrying a token in the command line.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, with the harness owning the boundary. Claude Code owns the connection, the one-time project-server approval prompt and the per-tool permission prompt on first call; the model owns only which tool it calls and when. The OAuth grant belongs to the individual user, not to the repository.
sheets.context_boundary: The server runs out of process, so only tool names, schemas and returned tool results cross into the session. That crossing is not free: each connected server's tool names and server instructions load into every session, so an unused server is a standing context tax and tool output should be bounded rather than dumped.
sheets.lifecycle: Claude Code reads .mcp.json at session start, so an edit needs a session restart; a project-scoped server shows as pending until the user approves it once, and shows Needs authentication until the /mcp Authenticate flow completes in the browser. The grant then persists for that user until it expires or the server is removed, and it stops applying entirely if the marketplace entry or the config file goes away.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open, and quietly. A server that does not connect leaves the session running with the status Failed to connect or Needs authentication and no tools, and from inside the conversation an absent tool is indistinguishable from a tool that declined, so Claude falls back to whatever is in context, which is the pasting behaviour you were trying to eliminate. The startup timeout is 30 seconds by default (raise it with MCP_TIMEOUT), and a token that expires mid-week degrades the same way.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on basic http MCP, but two build-specific details matter: as of v2.1.191 a 404 from an http server reports the URL it tried, where earlier builds show a generic POST error, and after testing a project-scope approval you must re-arm the prompt with claude mcp reset-project-choices. Servers using a static token instead of OAuth take it at add time with --header.

scenarios.scenario: Every session opened in this repo should begin already knowing the current sprint's ticket list and the active git branch, pulled live at that moment from our tooling, without anyone asking for it or pasting it in.

key.primary: A SessionStart hook (type: command) that runs the queries and returns the results via hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext so they are injected into the session's context
key.rejected_alternative: Adding the sprint and branch information to the project CLAUDE.md
key.rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md is static text loaded from disk; it cannot execute commands, so the sprint list and branch would be stale the moment they change and would need manual editing. The hooks reference lists SessionStart's purpose as loading development context, with a git-branch injection as its worked example.
key.lifecycle: Fires on the SessionStart event (startup, resume, clear, compact); command output is injected before the first user turn is processed
key.failure_mode: The CLAUDE.md version silently serves last sprint's tickets and the wrong branch until a human remembers to hand-edit the file, which is worse than no context because the model trusts it

sheets.primary: A SessionStart hook declared in project settings.json that runs a script which queries the tracker and shells out to git for the current branch, then emits that summary so the harness injects it as additional context at the top of the session. The script does the fetching; the model receives already-assembled text.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Recording the sprint list in CLAUDE.md. Rejected because CLAUDE.md is static text on disk that goes stale the moment the sprint or branch changes, and the requirement is explicitly live data at session open.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. It runs the hook deterministically on the session-start event and injects whatever the script returns; the model has no say in whether the lookup happens.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in its own process with no model context at all. Only its stdout, or the additional-context field of its JSON output, crosses into the main session context, where it sits as a one-time preamble for the rest of that conversation. Nothing flows the other way.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires once per session-start event; matchers distinguish a fresh start from resume and clear, so decide deliberately whether a resumed session should refetch. The injected text is a snapshot and stops being accurate the moment the branch is switched or a ticket moves, which the model will not notice on its own.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open: if the tracker is unreachable, the token is stale, or the script exceeds the hook timeout, the session starts anyway with no sprint context and nobody is told. Worse in practice is silent staleness, where the model confidently cites a branch the developer switched away from an hour ago. It also adds its token cost to every single session in the repo, including the many that do not care about sprint state, so keep the payload to a handful of lines.
sheets.version_caveat: The SessionStart event, its matcher values, and the JSON field used to inject additional context were all added and then adjusted across releases, and I cannot state the version or the exact field name with confidence. The hook timeout default is also version dependent; verify against the installed build rather than trusting a remembered value.

sheets.primary: A SessionStart hook of type "command" in the repo's .claude/settings.json, matched on startup|resume|clear|compact, that shells out to the tracker CLI and git, and returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext containing the sprint ticket list and the current branch.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md - it is the right home for static project facts and loads automatically, but it cannot execute anything, so it can never carry a sprint list that is correct at the moment the session opens.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code runs the hook before the first turn and splices its stdout into the conversation; the model does not choose whether the context arrives.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook process runs entirely outside the context window with the session JSON on stdin. Only the additionalContext string crosses in, at the start of the conversation, so keep it to a compact list rather than a full API dump.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs at session start and again on resume, /clear, compaction and forks, per the matcher you set. The injected text is an ordinary early conversation turn, so it goes stale as the session runs and can be dropped by compaction unless the compact matcher re-injects it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and silently. SessionStart cannot block, so if the tracker is down or the credential has expired the session starts anyway with no sprint context and nothing tells the user - the model then confidently works from nothing. It also puts a network round trip on the critical path of every single session start, so it must be fast and time-bounded.
sheets.version_caveat: SessionStart supports only the command and mcp_tool handler types, not http, prompt or agent. Its other output fields (initialUserMessage, sessionTitle, watchPaths, reloadSkills) are available on the same event. Hooks run without a controlling terminal from v2.1.139, so the script must not try to prompt.

sheets.primary: Hook: a SessionStart handler (command type) that queries the tracker and reads the branch, then returns the result as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext so it is added to Claude's context before the first prompt. The axis is behaviour tied to a lifecycle moment plus a live fetch, which no instruction file can perform.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md, which loads every session but can only carry text someone wrote earlier.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the firing: the hook runs at session start whether or not anyone asks. The model owns what it does with the injected text, which is ordinary context and carries no obligation.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler executes as a separate process outside the model's window; the tracker credentials, the API call and the parsing all stay there. Only the additionalContext string crosses into the session, so keep it a compact list rather than a raw API dump, and treat the returned ticket text as untrusted input rather than instructions.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs once per session on the SessionStart event, with the source reported as startup, resume, clear, compact or fork, and then never again for that session. That is the sharp edge: the snapshot is taken at launch, so a long-running session keeps a stale branch and a stale ticket list until someone starts a new one.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and silent. SessionStart has no blocking or decision control at all; an exit code 2 renders as a hook error notice in the transcript that Claude never sees, and the session proceeds normally. So a down tracker or an expired token produces a session that simply does not know the sprint, with nothing in context to signal the gap.
sheets.version_caveat: SessionStart's hookSpecificOutput is not context-only: it also accepts initialUserMessage, watchPaths, sessionTitle and reloadSkills, and initialUserMessage applies in non-interactive -p mode where it creates the first turn rather than attaching to one. Confirm the event and the handler type on the installed build before relying on any of those.

sheets.primary: A `SessionStart` hook registered in the repo's `.claude/settings.json`, matching `startup|resume|clear|compact|fork`, that shells out to the sprint tooling and `git`, then returns the result as `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext`. That string is injected as a system reminder at the start of the conversation, before the first prompt.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project CLAUDE.md section listing the tickets and branch. It loses because CLAUDE.md is static text read from disk, so it cannot be pulled live at session open and goes stale the moment the sprint board or the branch changes.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the trigger: Claude Code runs the hook at the lifecycle event regardless of what the model wants. The model owns only what it does with the injected text, which is ordinary context.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook process runs entirely outside the context window and inherits the user's environment and credentials. Only the `additionalContext` string crosses into the main session, as a system reminder rather than a chat message, and it is combined with output from any other SessionStart hooks.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on new session, on `--resume`/`--continue`/`/resume`, on `/clear`, after compaction, and on fork. It runs on every session, so it must be fast; the injected context persists through that session but not across resume, because hooks re-run on resume.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. SessionStart is non-blocking, so a slow, failing, or timed-out hook does not stop the session, it just starts with no sprint context and no loud signal. Output is capped at 10,000 characters, with the overflow written to a file and replaced by a preview plus path, and a long-running session keeps the snapshot it started with while the real board moves on.
sheets.version_caveat: SessionStart supports only `type: "command"` and `type: "mcp_tool"` handlers, not HTTP, prompt, or agent handlers. Hooks in project settings are subject to workspace trust, and an administrator setting `allowManagedHooksOnly` can suppress user and project hooks entirely.

scenarios.scenario: The platform team maintains a code-review helper, several lifecycle automations, and a tracker integration that about 40 repos across the org should all receive, with the ability to ship versioned updates that reach every consumer.

key.primary: A plugin (skills, agents, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json in one directory with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest) distributed through a plugin marketplace, private for internal use
key.rejected_alternative: Committing copies of the .claude/ directory (skills, agents, hooks in settings.json) into each of the 40 repositories
key.rejection_reason: The plugins doc draws this exact line: standalone .claude/ is for single-project and personal customization, plugins are for 'sharing with teammates, distributing to community, versioned releases, reusable across projects.' The manifest's version field plus marketplace installation gives controlled updates; namespacing prevents collisions.
key.lifecycle: Installed once from the marketplace per user or declared at repo level; components load whenever the plugin is enabled; bumping the manifest version propagates updates
key.failure_mode: The copy-paste approach drifts immediately: fixes must be re-copied into 40 repos, each copy mutates independently, and hook configs embedded in per-repo settings.json fall out of sync with the scripts they call

sheets.primary: One plugin containing skills/ for the code-review helper, hooks/hooks.json for the lifecycle automations and .mcp.json for the tracker integration, published through a private git marketplace and pinned with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Each consuming repo declares extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins in its .claude/settings.json, or the org pushes both through managed settings so it installs at managed scope.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into all 40 repos - it works for one project but has no version handle and no update path, so shipping a fix means 40 pull requests.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns discovery, installation, versioning and loading of the bundle. Ownership of the individual outcomes then splits: the hooks are harness-enforced, the code-review skill is model-invoked and advisory.
sheets.context_boundary: The plugin's components load into each consuming session's own context. Skill descriptions and the MCP server's tool definitions cost window every turn (the /plugin detail view shows a Context cost estimate); hook logic runs out-of-context in its own process.
sheets.lifecycle: Loads at session start once installed and enabled, and reloads on /reload-plugins. Consumers move to a new version when you bump plugin.json version and their marketplace auto-update runs (checked after session start with up to a ten-minute jitter, so the running session keeps its loaded version).
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open at the distribution layer, which is the real risk at 40 repos: a plugin that only a project settings.json enables and that comes from an external source does not load until the team member actually installs it, and Claude Code just reports it as not installed. Skew is the steady-state problem - some repos on old versions, some never reloaded - so treat managed settings as the only path if you need a guarantee rather than a nudge.
sheets.version_caveat: Omitting version makes the git commit SHA the version, so every commit counts as an update; set it explicitly. The per-load install requirement is v2.1.195+; "Will install" component listing is v2.1.145+, context cost v2.1.143+, last-updated v2.1.144+. Admins can set autoUpdate on each extraKnownMarketplaces entry and restrict sources with strictKnownMarketplaces. Plugin skills are namespaced /plugin-name:skill-name.

sheets.primary: Plugin, distributed through a marketplace the platform team owns: bundle the review skill, the lifecycle hooks and the tracker MCP server into one versioned plugin, publish .claude-plugin/marketplace.json from an internal git repo, and have each of the 40 repos declare extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins in its committed .claude/settings.json. The axis is distribution, versioning and rollback, which is the plugin layer's entire reason to exist.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude/ directory of skills, agents and hooks into each of the 40 repositories.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns packaging and loading (install, enable, namespacing, version resolution, and managed scope that users cannot modify), but inside the bundle the only enforcement point is the bundled hook. The review helper remains a skill, so its outcome is still the model's.
sheets.context_boundary: Per component, not per plugin: the skill body loads in the main session on invoke, the hooks run out of process, the MCP server runs out of process. What is unavoidable is the always-on listing cost the plugin adds to every session in every repo, which the plugin details view reports as a context cost estimate before install.
sheets.lifecycle: Consumers add the marketplace once (/plugin marketplace add owner/repo) and install by name, or get prompted to install when they trust the repository folder because the project settings declare it. Updates land through /plugin marketplace update or background auto-update, which runs after session start with a random delay of up to ten minutes and then asks for /reload-plugins; the running session keeps the versions it loaded at launch. Removing the marketplace uninstalls its plugins.
sheets.failure_mode: The bundle fails closed at load, all or nothing: a rejected manifest or a broken component means none of the three ship. Per consumer it fails silently instead, because a plugin that only the project's settings enable and that comes from an external source does not load until each member actually installs it, and Claude Code reports it as not installed rather than erroring. A pinned version also means pushed commits never reach installed users until the pin moves.
sheets.version_caveat: Pin a tag or branch by appending #ref when adding the marketplace, or teammates track a moving branch. The install-on-every-load-path behaviour applies as of v2.1.195, and enable/disable for plugins whose marketplace name and plugin.json name differ also needs v2.1.195; the uninstall scope dialog needs v2.1.203. Administrators can install at managed scope, which users cannot modify.

sheets.primary: A plugin, published through a plugin marketplace repository the platform team owns, bundling all three pieces: the code-review helper as a skill or command, the lifecycle automations as hook definitions, and the tracker integration as an MCP server entry. Consumer repos install from that marketplace and pick up versioned updates from one place instead of forty copied .claude directories.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A shared git submodule or a sync script that copies a .claude directory into each repo. Rejected because there is no version identity, no install or uninstall story, and drift is invisible until something breaks in one of the forty repos.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns loading and version resolution once a repo has the plugin enabled. Whether all forty repos actually adopt and update it is an organizational question, unless it is pushed via managed or enterprise policy settings, in which case the harness owns that too.
sheets.context_boundary: The marketplace repo lives entirely outside any session. In each consumer session the plugin's components load into that session's own context on the normal terms for their kind: skill descriptions resident and bodies on demand, hooks running out of context in their own processes, MCP tool schemas resident once connected.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from the moment a user or a policy enables the plugin in a repo, and updates when the marketplace is refreshed and the plugin updated. It stops applying on uninstall or disable. Version pinning matters: without it, forty repos can be running forty different snapshots.
sheets.failure_mode: Version drift is the standing failure, since a marketplace publish does not force consumers to update unless enterprise-managed settings pre-enable the plugin. Load failures tend to be quiet, so a repo can silently be running without the review helper. And a single bad publish now reaches forty repos at once, so the hook components in particular need a staged rollout, because a broken PreToolUse hook can block work everywhere simultaneously.
sheets.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces were introduced as a beta feature and I do not know the exact version that made them generally available, nor the current exact key names for pre-enabling plugins and extra marketplaces in managed settings. Confirm both against the installed release before promising forty teams a rollout mechanism.

sheets.primary: One plugin that bundles all three concerns: the review helper as a skill under `skills/`, the lifecycle automations as `hooks/hooks.json`, and the tracker integration as `.mcp.json` at the plugin root, with an explicit `version` in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. Distribute it through a marketplace hosted in a private org repository, and force-enable it for the 40 repos through managed settings.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone `.claude/` configuration copied into each repo. It loses on distribution: there is no install or update path, so a fix has to be hand-copied 40 times and the fleet drifts.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Mixed, and the split matters: the harness owns installation, enablement, and the hooks the plugin ships (they fire on their events), while the model owns the skill, which is instructions it interprets. Managed settings can force-enable or force-disable a plugin, and `--plugin-dir` cannot override that.
sheets.context_boundary: Each consumer's own session. Plugin skill descriptions and MCP tool names load into that session at start, full skill bodies on use, and hooks run outside the context window entirely. Plugin skills are namespaced as `/plugin-name:skill-name` so they cannot collide with a repo's local skills.
sheets.lifecycle: Installed once per consumer from the marketplace, then active in every session where the plugin is enabled. Consumers receive an update only when the platform team bumps the `version` field; if `version` is omitted and the plugin is distributed via git, the commit SHA is used and every commit counts as a new version. `/reload-plugins` picks up changes without a restart.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open, which is the real risk at 40 repos: a component that fails to load is skipped and the session starts anyway, with the problem visible only in the `/plugin` manager's Errors tab (an LSP or MCP server that fails to start appears there, an invalid configuration is silently skipped and needs `claude --debug`). A consumer who never updates stays on an old version indefinitely.
sheets.version_caveat: `--plugin-dir` accepting a `.zip` archive requires Claude Code v2.1.128 or later. Directory placement is a hard trap rather than a version one: only `plugin.json` goes inside `.claude-plugin/`, and `skills/`, `hooks/`, `agents/`, `.mcp.json` must sit at the plugin root. Plugin `settings.json` currently supports only the `agent` and `subagentStatusLine` keys.

scenarios.scenario: We scripted our production deploy as a repeatable procedure the assistant can execute, but it must only ever start when a human explicitly types the trigger. It must never begin because the assistant judged the code ready.

key.primary: A skill with disable-model-invocation: true in its frontmatter, invoked only as /deploy by the user
key.rejected_alternative: A regular skill with a description like 'deploys the application when the work is complete', relying on description matching plus a CLAUDE.md caution
key.rejection_reason: The skills doc names this case verbatim: use disable-model-invocation: true 'for workflows with side effects... like /commit, /deploy... You don't want Claude deciding to deploy because your code looks ready.' The flag removes the skill from the model's listing and blocks Skill-tool invocation, so only the human command path remains; a description-matched skill leaves the decision with the model.
key.lifecycle: Loads only when the user explicitly types /deploy; never surfaced to the model for automatic invocation
key.failure_mode: With a normal description-matched skill, a session where the user says 'looks done, wrap up' can match the description and trigger a real production deploy with no human decision in the loop

sheets.primary: Skill in explicit-invocation mode: .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md carrying the ordered procedure with disable-model-invocation set true, so the only entry point is a human typing /deploy. The axis is automatic invocation versus explicit user trigger, and the documented answer is a frontmatter setting on the same primitive rather than a different mechanism.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Dynamic Workflow in .claude/workflows/, which is also invoked as /name but exists for deterministic fan-out control flow and is reachable by the model through the Workflow tool.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and this matters. The harness owns the skill's entry point: with model invocation disabled the skill is removed from what Claude can trigger, including preload into subagents. It does not own the deploy itself, because the model can still run the underlying shell commands directly, so if the trigger must be the only path, add a PreToolUse hook or a permission deny rule on the deploy command.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session. The procedure text enters context only on the turn the user types /deploy, arguments substitute into it, and the body then stays for the rest of the session. Nothing about the skill is visible to the model beforehand.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on an explicit /deploy and on nothing else: no description match, no autonomous invocation, no subagent preload. It also works in non-interactive -p mode when /deploy is included in the prompt string, which is worth knowing because that is a path a script could take without a human. It stops applying when the session ends.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory once it starts, and only a partial guard before that. It fails open around the edges: the model that decides the code is ready can execute the same commands without ever touching the skill, so the flag prevents accidental skill invocation, not accidental deployment. A second trap is leaving a legacy .claude/commands/deploy.md alongside the skill, where one name shadows the other.
sheets.version_caveat: Invocation control is a Claude Code extension to the Agent Skills open standard, not part of the base standard, so the behaviour does not carry to other tools that read the same SKILL.md. The .claude/commands/ flat-file form is the legacy format and .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md is the recommended one; both still produce /deploy.

sheets.primary: A user-invoked skill, `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md`, with `disable-model-invocation: true` in the frontmatter. That flag hides the skill from Claude entirely, so its description never enters context and the model cannot decide to run it; the procedure exists only behind a human typing `/deploy`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The same procedure as an ordinary model-invocable skill. It loses because by default skill descriptions load at session start precisely so Claude can decide when to use them, which is the one behavior this deploy must not have.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the trigger: with `disable-model-invocation: true` the skill is invisible to Claude until the user invokes it, so the guarantee is structural rather than instructed. The model owns everything after that, namely executing the steps.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context window. Nothing at all crosses the boundary until invocation (context cost is zero for user-only skills), then the full body loads into the main conversation and stays for the rest of the session.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs only when the user types `/deploy`; it is never matched against a prompt and never auto-loaded. It applies from that invocation until the session ends or the context is cleared.
sheets.failure_mode: The gate is on invocation, not on the actions, so it fails open on execution fidelity: once a human triggers it the model runs the steps with the session's normal permissions and can improvise, skip, or reorder. The docs recommend this flag specifically for skills with side effects, but pairing it with PreToolUse hooks or deny rules on the irreversible steps is what makes the deploy itself safe.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate or plan restriction documented. If the procedure ever ships as someone else's skill, `skillOverrides` in settings applies the same hiding without editing the skill file. Note that `disable-model-invocation` is a Claude Code extension to the Agent Skills standard rather than part of the portable standard.

sheets.primary: A skill (deploy) whose frontmatter sets disable-model-invocation: true, so it is excluded from the model-invocable toolkit and exists only as the slash command /deploy that a human types. The ordered procedure and any helper scripts live in the skill directory.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A subagent for deploys - it packages the procedure just as well, but the main agent can spawn one on its own judgement, which is precisely the trigger condition you are trying to remove.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness enforces the entry point: with disable-model-invocation set, the skill is not offered to the model and it cannot invoke it. The model owns everything after the human types the command.
sheets.context_boundary: Main session context. Nothing of the skill body crosses in until the human invokes it; then the SKILL.md body plus any $ARGUMENTS enter context and the helper scripts run as subprocesses whose stdout comes back.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts only on an explicit human /deploy in the interactive session, and stops applying when that turn's procedure completes. It is not reachable from a subagent's or a teammate's own reasoning.
sheets.failure_mode: The gate is hard but narrow, so it fails open around the edges: nothing stops the model from running the underlying kubectl/terraform/deploy commands directly without going through the skill. Pair it with permissions.ask or permissions.deny rules on the actual deploy commands so the procedure is the only approved path, not merely the only named one.
sheets.version_caveat: disable-model-invocation is a Claude Code extension to the Agent Skills standard, not part of the portable spec. In a headless run, --disable-slash-commands turns off all skills and commands, so a CI wrapper would silently lose the entry point. Skills in a plugin are invoked namespaced as /plugin-name:deploy.

sheets.primary: A custom slash command, a markdown file under .claude/commands/, holding the deploy procedure, with its frontmatter narrowing the tools it may use. A command exists only as an expansion of something a human typed, so there is no path by which the model reaches it on its own initiative.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill containing the same procedure. Rejected for exactly the property that makes skills good elsewhere: the model decides when a skill applies, so a skill described as the deploy procedure can be self-invoked the moment the model concludes the code looks ready.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and this needs saying plainly. The harness owns the trigger, since only user input expands a command. The model owns the execution of the steps once expanded, and it can deviate, skip a step, or improvise on an error.
sheets.context_boundary: The command file's text is substituted into the user turn of the main session context, so the whole procedure becomes resident from that point. Any bash pre-execution in the command runs outside context and only its output is inlined. There is no separate context window unless a step delegates to a subagent.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when a human types it, and applies for the duration of that turn's work. It has no standing effect; nothing about it persists into later turns beyond the transcript.
sheets.failure_mode: The trigger is genuinely closed, but the containment is not: nothing in this mechanism stops the model from running the same deploy script directly during ordinary work, since the prohibition lives only in the command's existence. If the real requirement is that production deploys cannot start without a human, back it with a PreToolUse hook that denies the deploy command or script unless a marker set by the slash command is present. On its own the choice is advisory once execution starts, and a mid-procedure error leaves the model improvising against production.
sheets.version_caveat: Slash commands are long-standing and low-risk. I am not certain which frontmatter keys the installed version supports (allowed-tools, argument-hint, model and similar have varied), so verify the frontmatter parses rather than assuming, and note that a key an older build does not recognize may be ignored silently rather than erroring.

scenarios.scenario: Whenever a new issue is opened in our GitHub repository, we want it triaged automatically: labeled, checked against likely duplicates, and given a first-response comment, with no human at a terminal anywhere in the loop.

key.primary: The Claude Code GitHub Action (anthropics/claude-code-action@v1) in a workflow triggered on issues: [opened], with the triage instructions in the prompt input (automation mode)
key.rejected_alternative: A hook, on the theory that hooks are the event-driven automation mechanism
key.rejection_reason: Hooks fire on Claude Code lifecycle events inside a running session (PreToolUse, SessionStart, Stop, and so on); no session exists when a GitHub issue is opened, so there is no event to hook. The GitHub Action is the documented mechanism for repo-event automation: it works with any GitHub event trigger and runs immediately when a prompt is supplied.
key.lifecycle: GitHub webhook (issues: opened) starts a workflow run; each run is a fresh non-interactive Claude Code execution on a CI runner
key.failure_mode: The hook version simply never runs: nothing in the repo listens to GitHub webhooks, so issues sit untriaged while the config looks superficially plausible
key.version_caveat: Use action @v1: the beta inputs (mode:, direct_prompt:, custom_instructions:) were removed in v1.0; mode is auto-detected and CLI options move into claude_args

sheets.primary: A GitHub Action using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 in a workflow triggered on: issues: types: [opened], with a prompt input describing the triage (label, search for duplicates, post a first response). Supplying prompt puts the action in automation mode, which runs immediately rather than waiting for an @claude mention.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A self-hosted headless Agent SDK service reacting to the issues webhook - it gives more control but you rebuild runner provisioning, checkout, token minting and GitHub API plumbing that the action already provides.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness in the broad sense: GitHub Actions decides that the run happens at all, on the webhook event, with no model involvement. The quality of the labelling and duplicate call is the model's, and it is unreviewed.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh, ephemeral context on the GitHub-hosted runner, one per workflow run, sharing nothing with any developer session. In: the issue title and body, repo CLAUDE.md, whatever it queries through the GitHub API. Out: label mutations and a comment, plus the job log.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on the issues.opened webhook and ends when the job finishes, hits --max-turns (default 10) or the workflow timeout. It applies to every new issue from the moment the workflow file merges until it is removed or disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open: a failed or skipped job leaves the issue untriaged and nobody is watching a terminal, so add job-failure alerting. The sharper risk is that issue bodies are attacker-controlled text flowing straight into an agent holding contents/issues/pull-requests write - keep the token scoped, keep --allowedTools tight, and treat mislabelling and false duplicate calls as expected.
sheets.version_caveat: v1 is GA and has breaking changes from @beta: mode is removed and auto-detected, direct_prompt became prompt, and max_turns/model/custom_instructions/allowed_tools all moved into claude_args. Needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in repo secrets (or Bedrock/Vertex OIDC with use_bedrock/use_vertex), the Claude GitHub App installed by a repo admin, and contents/issues/pull-requests read-write plus id-token: write for the cloud variants.

sheets.primary: A GitHub Action workflow triggered on the issues opened event, running Claude Code headlessly in the runner (the official Claude Code action, or a plain claude -p invocation) with a prompt to label, search for duplicates and post a first response, and with tool access narrowed to the gh CLI or the GitHub API calls it needs. No terminal and no human is involved anywhere.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A local hook or a scheduled polling job on someone's machine. Rejected because it depends on a workstation being awake and a session existing, which contradicts the no-human-at-a-terminal requirement, and because the natural trigger is a webhook the platform already delivers.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split by layer. The harness, meaning GitHub Actions, owns whether the job runs at all and what credentials it has. The model owns the triage judgment, and there is no mechanism that makes a label choice correct.
sheets.context_boundary: Each run is a fresh, ephemeral context in the runner, with no memory of prior issues. What crosses in is the event payload, the checked-out repo, and whatever the prompt fetches; what crosses out is the API side effects (labels, comment) and the job log. Nothing carries to the next run unless it is written to the repo or an issue.
sheets.lifecycle: One run per issues opened event, and it ends when the job ends. It stops applying if the workflow file is removed, the trigger is disabled, or the API credential secret is revoked or exhausted.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in the useful sense that an errored job leaves the issue untriaged rather than mislabeled, but the real risk is prompt injection: the issue body is fully attacker-controlled text being fed to an agent that holds a write-capable token, so a crafted issue can try to drive comments, labels or worse. Constrain the token to issues write only, never grant contents write or secrets access in this workflow, and expect non-deterministic labeling and occasional confidently wrong duplicate calls.
sheets.version_caveat: The official Claude Code GitHub Action has gone through breaking input changes between its beta and v1 style interfaces and I cannot state the current input names or the correct tag to pin. It requires an API credential secret (direct Anthropic key, or Bedrock or Vertex configuration) and consumes paid usage per issue, which is a plan and budget consideration, not just a version one.

sheets.primary: A GitHub Action workflow using `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`, triggered `on: issues: types: [opened]`, with a `prompt` input carrying the triage instructions. Supplying `prompt` puts the action in automation mode, which runs immediately rather than waiting for an `@claude` mention, so no human is in the loop.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Claude Code hook. It loses on the premise: hooks fire on lifecycle events inside a running Claude Code session, and there is no session and nobody at a terminal when a GitHub issue is opened.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, in two layers: GitHub Actions deterministically starts the job on the webhook event, and the action's own auto-detection picks automation mode. The model owns triage quality only, the labels it picks, the duplicates it finds, and the comment it writes.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh, ephemeral context on a GitHub-hosted runner, one per workflow run, with no carry-over between issues. The issue body and whatever the workflow checks out cross in; labels, duplicate findings, and the first-response comment cross out through the GitHub API. Repository CLAUDE.md is picked up when the workflow checks the repo out.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on the configured webhook event and ends when the job finishes, when `--max-turns` is reached (default 10), or when the workflow-level timeout fires. Nothing persists to the next issue.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. If the job errors, the API key is missing or invalid, or the turn budget runs out, the issue simply sits untriaged and the only signal is a red check in Actions. The workflow needs Contents, Issues, and Pull requests read-write plus `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in repository secrets, and because issue text is attacker-controlled input, a crafted issue body is prompt-injection surface for a job that comments and labels automatically.
sheets.version_caveat: v1.0 is GA and introduces breaking changes from `@beta`: `mode` is removed and auto-detected, `direct_prompt` becomes `prompt`, and `max_turns`, `model`, `custom_instructions`, `allowed_tools` all move into `claude_args`. The `/install-github-app` quick setup is only available to direct Claude API users; Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud require the manual OIDC path. Being able to stop at App installation with **Skip for now** requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later.

sheets.primary: Claude Code GitHub Action: a workflow in .github/workflows using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1, triggered by on: issues: types: [opened], with an explicit prompt input so the action runs in automation mode instead of waiting for an @claude mention, and issues: write permission so it can label and comment. This is the CI tier, the only place where no human is at a terminal at all.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A custom Agent SDK service listening on a GitHub webhook, which reproduces the runner, the auth and the retry handling for the same outcome.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, in the CI sense: GitHub Actions decides when the job runs, and the permission model is the workflow's and the GitHub App's rather than anyone's local settings. The model owns triage quality, which labels it picks and which issues it calls duplicates.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh ephemeral Claude Code session per issue, on a GitHub-hosted runner. Only what the workflow supplies crosses in: the checked-out repository (including CLAUDE.md), the prompt with GitHub context variables, and whatever claude_args allow. Only the posted labels and comment cross out; nothing carries to the next run.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on the issues.opened webhook and ends when the job returns or hits the --max-turns cap or the workflow timeout. It stops applying if the workflow file is removed, the Claude GitHub App is uninstalled, or the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY secret is deleted or invalid.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory with respect to the issue and fails open: a bad key, a missing permission or a failed run leaves the issue untriaged and blocks nothing. The subtler failure is the trigger shape, since for events that are not comments Claude responds only to the trigger phrase unless you pass prompt, so an issue-opened workflow without a prompt silently does nothing. Wrong labels and wrong duplicate calls are posted publicly with no human check.
sheets.version_caveat: v1.0 is a breaking change from the beta: mode is removed and auto-detected, direct_prompt becomes prompt, and max_turns, model, custom_instructions, allowed_tools and disallowed_tools all move into claude_args. You must be a repository admin to install the app and add secrets, and the /install-github-app quickstart path is for direct Claude API users (Bedrock and Google Cloud need the OIDC setup); its Skip for now option needs Claude Code v2.1.187 or later.

scenarios.scenario: A production bug has five plausible root causes. We want five investigators working simultaneously, each defending one hypothesis and actively trying to disprove the others' findings through direct back-and-forth, converging on a written consensus.

key.primary: An agent team: enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, then have the lead spawn five teammates who share the task list and message each other directly over the mailbox system
key.rejected_alternative: Spawning five parallel subagents from the main session, one per hypothesis
key.rejection_reason: The agent-teams doc's comparison table is decisive: subagents 'report results back to the main agent only' and 'never talk to each other,' while teammates 'message each other directly' and self-coordinate on a shared task list. The requirement is peer-to-peer challenge, which subagents structurally cannot do; the docs even use competing-hypotheses debugging as the canonical team example.
key.lifecycle: Gated behind the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 env var or settings entry; team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate with user approval; cleanup on session end
key.failure_mode: With subagents, each investigator reports one plausible theory to the orchestrator and no cross-examination ever happens; anchoring survives and the synthesized answer is just the first convincing hypothesis
key.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Behavior described as of v2.1.178 (TeamCreate/TeamDelete removed); known limitations include no /resume of in-process teammates and one team per session

sheets.primary: An agent team: the main session acts as lead and spawns five teammates, each assigned one hypothesis, instructed to message each other directly and try to disprove the others' theories, with the surviving consensus written to a findings document. This is the documented competing-hypotheses use case for teams.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five Task subagents - they parallelise the investigation but architecturally cannot talk to each other; each only reports back to the main agent, so the adversarial cross-examination you want never happens.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model, at every level. The harness supplies the mailbox files, the shared task list and file-locked task claiming; whether the debate actually happens, and whether the consensus is real rather than premature agreement, is entirely the lead's and teammates' judgement.
sheets.context_boundary: Five separate context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills fresh but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so the spawn prompt must carry the case facts. What crosses between them are SendMessage payloads, task-list state and the findings file on disk.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate and is scoped to that one session. Teammates end on shutdown request or session exit; the team config directory is removed automatically at session end while the task list persists under cleanupPeriodDays.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and expensive. Token cost scales roughly linearly with teammate count, the lead often declares consensus before the work is done, teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete and block dependents, and a teammate that hits an API error can stop instead of recovering. Note also that a teammate cannot approve a permission prompt for another - relayed approvals are treated as untrusted input.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default: set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json env or the environment, or nothing spawns at all. Behaviour described is v2.1.178+, where TeamCreate/TeamDelete no longer exist and team_name on the Agent tool is ignored. Known limits: one team per session, no nested teams, no restoration of in-process teammates on /resume, and split-pane mode needs tmux or iTerm2 with it2.

sheets.primary: An agent team: five peer agents, each seeded with one hypothesis and instructed to attack the others, with a coordinating lead that holds the shared record and writes the consensus document. The load-bearing requirement is direct back-and-forth between the investigators, which needs a mechanism where agents can address each other, not just report upward.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched with the Task tool. Rejected because subagents are isolated: each has its own context, none can see or message another, and every result funnels back only to the orchestrator, so the adversarial cross-examination the scenario asks for degrades into five independent reports the lead has to reconcile alone.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model, overwhelmingly. The harness only spawns the agents and routes messages between them; whether the debate is genuinely adversarial and whether the consensus is sound are model behaviours no configuration can enforce.
sheets.context_boundary: Each investigator holds its own separate context window, which is the entire point, since it keeps five hypotheses from contaminating each other. Only explicit messages cross between them, plus whatever they read and write on the shared filesystem. The consensus document is the durable artifact, and it should be a file rather than a chat summary, because everything in those five contexts is discarded when they end.
