sheets.lifecycle: Spawned deliberately for this one investigation, running until the consensus file is written or the lead terminates them. Nothing about it persists afterwards; a follow-up question starts from the written document, not the agents.
sheets.failure_mode: Cost multiplies by roughly the number of agents and each of them is re-billing its own accumulated context every turn, so a long debate is expensive out of proportion to the answer. Behaviourally the common failure is premature agreement, where agents concede to each other rather than defend, producing a consensus that is social rather than evidential; the opposite failure is a message loop that never converges. Five agents writing to the same files without coordination will also clobber each other. It fails open in every case: you get a document either way, and its confidence is not correlated with its correctness.
sheets.version_caveat: Multi-agent teams with direct agent-to-agent messaging are a recent and, as far as I know, still-evolving capability, and I cannot state the version that introduced them, whether they are behind a flag, or the exact name of the messaging tool in the installed build. If the installed version has only Task-style subagents, this design is not available and the fallback is the orchestrator manually relaying each agent's findings to the others in successive rounds, which is slower and loses the simultaneity.

sheets.primary: Agent Teams: spawn five teammates from the lead session, one hypothesis each, instructed to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories, with the shared task list tracking who owns what and the surviving theory written to a findings document. The axis is independent peers that communicate directly, and the docs name competing-hypothesis debugging as a primary use case.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five subagents, which have their own context windows but report only to the main agent and never talk to each other.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead owns decomposition, task assignment and the final synthesis, and it approves teammate plans autonomously without prompting you. The only harness levers over the debate are hooks: TeammateIdle, TaskCreated and TaskCompleted can exit 2 to send feedback and refuse an idle or a completion.
sheets.context_boundary: Five independent Claude Code sessions, each with its own context window. A teammate loads the same project context as a normal session (CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, skills) plus the lead's spawn prompt, but the lead's conversation history does not carry over. What crosses between them is only peer messages, delivered through per-agent mailbox files, and the shared task list.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate, which happens only after you ask or after you approve a proposal. It runs until teammates are shut down or go idle, and the team config directory is cleaned up automatically when the session exits, while the task list persists locally. /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and stalls rather than erroring. Teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete, which blocks dependents; a teammate that hits an error may stop instead of recovering; the lead may decide the team is finished before the work is; and two teammates editing one file overwrite each other. Nothing enforces that a real consensus was reached, so the written conclusion is whatever the lead synthesised, which is exactly the anchoring the design is meant to avoid.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default: it needs CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS set to 1 in settings.json or the environment, and without it no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The implicit lifecycle described here is v2.1.178 and later, where TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist. Hard limits: one team per session, no nested teams, the lead is fixed, teammates do not inherit the lead's /model, and token cost scales linearly with team size. Split panes need tmux or iTerm2 and are unsupported in Windows Terminal, VS Code and Ghostty.

sheets.primary: An agent team: the main session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, one per hypothesis, each a full independent Claude Code session, instructed to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories, with the surviving consensus written to a shared findings doc. This is the documented use case for debugging with competing hypotheses, and the adversarial debate is the mechanism that defeats anchoring.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five subagents. Both give isolated context windows, but subagents report results back to the main agent only and never talk to each other, so there is no direct back-and-forth and no way for one investigator to challenge another's finding.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead coordinates, assigns and synthesizes autonomously, and teammates self-claim work; the harness only supplies the plumbing (mailbox files, the file-locked shared task list, and the `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted` hooks you can use as quality gates).
sheets.context_boundary: Five separate context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, and skills like a normal session but does not inherit the lead's conversation history. What crosses between them is the spawn prompt, `SendMessage` messages delivered through `~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/`, the shared task list, and the findings file on disk.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned, after you approve, and is scoped to that one session; the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime. It ends when the session exits, at which point the team config directory is cleaned up automatically while the task list directory persists for resumed sessions under `cleanupPeriodDays`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and messily, and the documented limitations bite precisely on a five-way converging investigation: task status lags when teammates fail to mark work complete, which blocks dependent tasks; the lead may declare the team finished before the work is; teammates stop on errors instead of recovering; `/resume` and `/rewind` do not restore in-process teammates; and token cost scales linearly with five separate Claude instances.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default. They require `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in settings.json or the environment; without it no team is set up and Claude will not spawn or propose teammates. The documented behavior is as of v2.1.178, where `TeamCreate` and `TeamDelete` no longer exist and `team_name` is deprecated; split-pane display needs tmux or iTerm2 with `it2` and is unsupported in VS Code's integrated terminal, Windows Terminal, and Ghostty.

scenarios.scenario: For a data-annotation project we want the assistant to act as a data analyst rather than a software engineer: every reply in a fixed tabular report format, with the default engineering behavior removed, applying to every turn of every interactive session in this project.

key.primary: A custom output style (.claude/output-styles/analyst.md without keep-coding-instructions), selected via /config or the outputStyle setting
key.rejected_alternative: Writing the persona and format rules into the project CLAUDE.md
key.rejection_reason: Output styles modify the system prompt itself and, by default, omit Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions; CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove those built-ins. The docs' comparison table assigns 'a different role, tone, or default response format every turn' to output styles and reserves CLAUDE.md for project conventions and codebase context.
key.lifecycle: Set once in settings (outputStyle) or via /config; read at session start, so changes take effect after /clear or a new session; applies to the main conversation only, not subagents
key.failure_mode: The CLAUDE.md version fights the still-present engineering system prompt: the assistant repeatedly drifts back to code-centric behavior and free-form answers, and the team keeps re-prompting for the report format
key.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; select styles through /config or the outputStyle setting instead

sheets.primary: A custom output style, stored under the project's .claude/output-styles/ and selected for this project, since an output style replaces the default software-engineering system prompt rather than appending to it. That replacement is the specific requirement here: the ask is not to add analyst instructions but to remove the engineering default, and no additive mechanism does that.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md instruction describing the analyst persona and the table format. Rejected because CLAUDE.md is layered on top of the default system prompt, so the engineering behaviour it is supposed to displace remains in force and competes with it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. An output style is still text in a system prompt, so nothing outside the model checks that a given reply is actually in the required table format.
sheets.context_boundary: It occupies the main agent's system prompt in the interactive session context, for every turn. It generally does not propagate to subagents, which keep their own prompts, and it is a property of the interactive configuration rather than of a headless invocation, so a CI or SDK run of the same project will not inherit it.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the style is selected and persists across sessions in that project because the selection is written to project settings, not to a single conversation. It stops applying when the style is switched back or the setting is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Purely advisory, and it fails open by drifting: over a long session the model gradually relaxes the fixed columns, especially when a turn does not fit the table shape (errors, clarifying questions). Removing the engineering default also removes conventions the tooling quietly relies on, so file edits and tool use can get sloppier. And because subagents and headless runs do not inherit it, output format becomes inconsistent the moment work is delegated.
sheets.version_caveat: Output styles were added mid-2025 in the 1.0.x line and I cannot pin the exact minimum version; the settings key that persists the selection has also changed name across releases in my recollection, so verify the value written by the interactive selector rather than hand-editing settings from memory. If the installed version lacks output styles, the closest fallback is a project CLAUDE.md, which is additive and therefore will not satisfy the remove-the-default half of this request.

sheets.primary: Custom output style: a Markdown file at .claude/output-styles/data-analyst.md defining the analyst role and the fixed tabular reply format, with keep-coding-instructions left out so the built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped rather than kept, and outputStyle set in the project's settings so everyone on the project gets it. This is the only authored surface that modifies the system prompt rather than adding context to it, which is what removing the default engineering behavior requires.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md, which adds a user message after the system prompt and can therefore add a format preference but cannot remove the engineering instructions.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness places the text into the system prompt and emits adherence reminders during the conversation, but nothing checks that a given reply actually came out as a table.
sheets.context_boundary: The main conversation only, for every turn of it. A subagent runs its own system prompt, so delegated work is unaffected by the style; a conversation fork is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt. Cost lands on input tokens, mitigated by prompt caching after the first request.
sheets.lifecycle: It applies from session start to session end, on every response, once selected via /config or the outputStyle setting. It is read once at session start, so an edit to the file, or a switch of style, takes effect only after /clear or a new session.
sheets.failure_mode: It cannot fail closed, because it is system-prompt text and not enforcement. The dangerous version is silent: if the style is not selected, not loaded, or overridden by an enabled plugin style using force-for-plugin, the session simply behaves as Default and announces nothing, which reads as a broken style when it merely was never loaded.
sheets.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; on current builds select through /config or set the outputStyle field directly. keep-coding-instructions defaults to false, which is the behaviour you want here. As of v2.1.178, when nested project .claude/output-styles directories define the same style name, the one closest to the working directory wins.

sheets.primary: A custom output style at .claude/output-styles/data-analyst.md that defines the analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with keep-coding-instructions left unset so Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped from the system prompt. Select it project-wide by setting outputStyle in .claude/settings.json rather than relying on the /config picker.
sheets.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md - it is added as a user message after the system prompt, so it can add analyst conventions but cannot remove the default engineering instructions, which is the explicit requirement here.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness assembles the system prompt and swaps the built-in engineering block out. Actually emitting the tabular format on each reply is the model's job, reinforced by the periodic adherence reminders output styles trigger.
sheets.context_boundary: The main conversation's system prompt only. It does not reach subagents, which run their own system prompts; a forked conversation is the exception because it inherits the parent's full system prompt. The added instructions cost input tokens once and are then served from the prompt cache.
sheets.lifecycle: Read once at session start and in force for every turn of that session. Changing it takes effect only after /clear or a new session, and it stops applying when the outputStyle setting changes or a plugin style with force-for-plugin overrides it.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory: it is still just system-prompt text, so on long or awkward turns the model drifts out of the strict table shape, and there is no harness check that a reply matched the format. Removing the coding instructions also degrades any incidental engineering work in the project, which is intended here but surprises people who expected a formatting change only.
sheets.version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91 - use /config or set outputStyle directly. Note that the /config picker writes to .claude/settings.local.json, which is per-developer and not shared, so a project-wide requirement must be committed in .claude/settings.json. As of v2.1.178 nested project output-style directories resolve to the one closest to the working directory.

sheets.primary: A custom output style: a markdown file in `.claude/output-styles/` describing the data-analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with `keep-coding-instructions` left out so it defaults to false. That omission is the load-bearing part, because a custom style leaves out Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions unless that field is set to true.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A project CLAUDE.md stating the persona and format. It loses because CLAUDE.md is added as a user message after the system prompt: it is purely additive and cannot remove the built-in engineering instructions the project wants gone.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. An output style modifies the system prompt directly and triggers adherence reminders during the conversation, but the response is still generated by the model, so this is stronger steering rather than harness enforcement.
sheets.context_boundary: The main conversation only, at the system-prompt level. The style is read once at session start, so a change takes effect after `/clear` or a new session. Subagents run their own system prompt and are unaffected; a fork is the exception, since it inherits the parent's full system prompt.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from session start once selected, on every turn, until the style is changed. Selection is made through `/config` and saved as `outputStyle` in `.claude/settings.local.json` at the local project level, or set by editing the `outputStyle` field in a settings file directly.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory. Adherence reminders help but the model can still drift out of the fixed table format on a long or unusual turn. Two structural gaps: the style does not reach subagents, so any delegated work reverts to engineering behavior, and the `/config` selection lands in `settings.local.json`, which is per-machine, so "every session in this project" requires committing the `outputStyle` setting or shipping the style in a plugin with `force-for-plugin: true`.
sheets.version_caveat: The standalone `/output-style` command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use `/config` or set `outputStyle` directly. As of v2.1.178, when nested `.claude/output-styles/` directories define a style with the same name, the one closest to the working directory wins.

scenarios.scenario: A CI job pipes each pull request diff to the assistant for a typo and lint pass. The output must be byte-for-byte reproducible no matter whose machine or which runner executes it; a teammate's personal automation or the project's tool-server config must not leak into the run.

key.primary: Headless invocation with bare mode: claude --bare -p with the prompt, --allowedTools for the needed tools, and any required context passed explicitly via flags
key.rejected_alternative: Plain claude -p in the CI script, reasoning that non-interactive mode is already isolated
key.rejection_reason: The headless docs state that without --bare, claude -p 'loads the same context an interactive session would,' including hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from the working directory and ~/.claude. Bare mode exists precisely for 'CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine': a hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or a server in the project's .mcp.json never runs because bare mode never reads them.
key.lifecycle: Explicitly invoked per CI run as a one-shot non-interactive command; only flags passed on that invocation take effect
key.failure_mode: Plain -p produces environment-dependent results: a developer's PostToolUse formatter hook or a project MCP server silently alters output on some machines, and the lint gate becomes flaky in a way that is nearly impossible to reproduce
key.version_caveat: --bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is slated to become the default for -p in a future release; until then, omitting it changes behavior

sheets.primary: A headless non-interactive run of the Claude Code CLI (the Agent SDK surface): claude -p with the diff on stdin, pinned with --strict-mcp-config (optionally alongside an explicit --mcp-config), --settings pointing at a settings file committed in the repo, --setting-sources restricted to project, --permission-mode dontAsk and an explicit --allowedTools, with --output-format json for a machine-readable result.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The anthropics/claude-code-action GitHub Action - a fine wrapper, but it is a convenience layer over the same headless invocation and does not itself pin away ambient configuration, so you would end up passing the identical isolation flags through claude_args anyway.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Every one of these is a CLI flag evaluated by Claude Code before the model runs; the model cannot re-enable a discarded MCP server or a suppressed user hook from inside the conversation.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh single-turn context per CI run on the runner, sharing nothing with any developer session. In: the diff plus the pinned system prompt and project settings. Out: the JSON result. Add --no-session-persistence so the run leaves no transcript on the runner.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the CI step executes, ends at the final response or --max-turns / --max-budget-usd. There is no turn boundary in headless mode, so denied actions stay denied for the rest of the run rather than resetting.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on configuration - --strict-mcp-config discards the project's .mcp.json servers and --bare or --safe-mode also skip auto-discovered hooks, skills, plugins and CLAUDE.md, so a lint pass that quietly depended on one of those just stops working. The bigger caveat is the premise: these flags make the *inputs* identical, not the *output*. Model sampling means byte-for-byte identical text is not something the CLI can promise, so the CI gate should assert on a normalised structured result, not on a diff of the raw reply.
sheets.version_caveat: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md; --safe-mode disables all customisations including workflows and themes - pick whichever matches how much of the project config you actually want. dontAsk mode auto-denies anything not pre-approved and never waits for input, which is the intended CI posture; in -p mode repeated blocks abort the run rather than falling back to prompting. --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections moves machine-specific text out of the system prompt, which also helps runner-to-runner consistency.

sheets.primary: A headless invocation in CI, either claude -p or an Agent SDK program, launched with every configuration source pinned explicitly: a checked-in settings file passed on the command line, MCP configuration passed explicitly with strict MCP mode so the ambient .mcp.json and the runner user's settings are ignored, an explicit allowed-tools list, and a pinned full model id rather than an alias. The prompt and the diff are the only inputs that vary.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A GitHub Action wrapper that just runs the assistant with default configuration discovery. Rejected because default discovery is exactly the leak being described: it merges user-level settings, project settings, local settings and any .mcp.json it finds, so the result depends on whose checkout and whose home directory the job lands in.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, for the isolation half: config precedence and the strict-config flags are enforced by the CLI, not by model good behaviour. Nobody owns the reproducibility half, which is the honest answer below.
sheets.context_boundary: Each run is a fresh ephemeral context in the runner containing only the pinned system configuration, the prompt and the diff. Nothing from a developer's machine, prior runs, or a conversation crosses in, and the only thing crossing out is the structured output the job captures.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs per pull request event or per push to the PR branch, and ends with the job. It carries no state between runs, which is a feature here: statelessness is part of what makes runs comparable.
sheets.failure_mode: The stated requirement cannot be fully met and should be pushed back on: byte-for-byte identical output from a language model is not guaranteed even with identical inputs, identical configuration and a pinned model, because sampling and serving-side variation are not under your control, and a model alias silently repointing makes it worse. Config isolation itself fails open and silently: omit the strict flag and the run quietly picks up the runner's ambient MCP servers and settings with no error, and you will not notice until outputs diverge. The durable fix is to let a real linter own the byte-exact, gating part and let the model output be advisory commentary that is never diffed for equality.
sheets.version_caveat: I am confident a strict MCP configuration flag exists that confines the run to explicitly passed MCP config, and that the Agent SDK grew an option controlling which filesystem setting sources are loaded (defaulting to loading none), but I cannot state either name or its version with certainty and both should be verified against the installed CLI and SDK. Pinning a dated full model id rather than an alias is the part I would not skip regardless of version.

sheets.primary: A headless CLI invocation (equivalently an Agent SDK run), `claude -p` with the config surface pinned shut: `--strict-mcp-config` so only servers from an explicit `--mcp-config` load and every other MCP source is ignored, `--setting-sources project` (omitting `user` and `local`) so no teammate's personal settings enter, plus `--settings` for the run's own overrides, an explicit `--model`, `--allowedTools`, and `--output-format json`. Check the invocation into the repo so the runner cannot vary it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Committing the desired configuration to `.claude/settings.json` and relying on that. It loses because settings layers merge: user-scope `~/.claude/settings.json` and a developer's `settings.local.json` still contribute unless the source list is explicitly restricted, which is exactly the leak described.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The flags are resolved by the client before the model is invoked, deciding which setting sources and which MCP servers exist at all; `--strict-mcp-config` makes Claude Code ignore all other MCP configurations, and `--settings` values override matching keys for that session only.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh, single-turn headless session per CI run, with no prior conversation and no persisted state. The diff goes in as the prompt; the structured JSON result comes out. Nothing from the operator's machine crosses in beyond what the pinned flags admit.
sheets.lifecycle: One invocation per pull request diff, starting when the CI job runs the command and ending when print mode exits after responding. Every flag applies to that session only, so nothing carries into the next run.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on omission, silently: drop `--strict-mcp-config` and the runner's `.mcp.json` and user-scope servers load anyway, and drop `--setting-sources` and personal settings merge back in, with no error either way. Worth stating plainly: the docs do not promise byte-identical output, since generation is sampled, so pinning the model and the config makes the run *reproducible in configuration* and the stable contract should be the output schema, not the exact bytes.
sheets.version_caveat: `--settings` must point at a regular file no larger than 2 MiB. `--setting-sources` takes a comma-separated list of `user`, `project`, `local`. There is a real version gate on the exclusion: before v2.1.211, rules that load on demand, including path-scoped rules and rules in nested `.claude/rules/` directories, loaded even when `project` was excluded from `--setting-sources`.

sheets.primary: Agent SDK in headless CLI form: pipe the diff into claude --bare -p with every option passed explicitly, for example git diff main | claude --bare -p "<typo linter instructions>" --allowedTools Read --output-format json. --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so only the flags in the CI script take effect; add --strict-mcp-config with --mcp-config, or --setting-sources, when the run genuinely needs some config but not all of it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A checked-in project Skill holding the lint procedure, since anything discovered from .claude/ or ~/.claude is precisely the ambient config the requirement excludes.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, for the part that can be owned. The isolation flags are startup-time filters the model cannot re-enable mid-run: --strict-mcp-config uses only servers from --mcp-config and ignores all other MCP configuration, and --setting-sources names exactly which of user, project and local load. The review content itself stays the model's.
sheets.context_boundary: A fresh non-interactive session per CI run, with the diff arriving on stdin (capped at 10 MB) and the verdict leaving on stdout. Under --bare nothing from a teammate's ~/.claude or the project's .mcp.json crosses in, because bare mode never reads them; with --output-format json the result carries session id, cost and the plugin_errors and mcp_server_errors arrays a CI gate can fail on.
sheets.lifecycle: It begins when the CI step runs the command and ends when the process exits; nothing persists between runs. A background Bash task the run started is terminated about five seconds after the final result, and a SIGTERM aborts the turn, runs SessionEnd hooks and exits with code 143.
sheets.failure_mode: Two different failures, and the first should be said out loud: byte-for-byte identical output is not achievable, because the model is not deterministic. What these flags buy is a reproducible configuration, not a reproducible string, so constrain the shape with --output-format json plus --json-schema and compare structured fields rather than raw text. The config leak fails open and silently: without --bare, claude -p loads the same context an interactive session would, including a teammate's ~/.claude hook or the project's .mcp.json, with no warning that the run was contaminated.
sheets.version_caveat: --bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is documented as becoming the default for -p in a future release, so pass it explicitly rather than relying on the current default. Bare mode also skips OAuth and keychain reads, so set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or an apiKeyHelper via --settings. Piped stdin has been capped at 10 MB since v2.1.128; before v2.1.205 an invalid --json-schema was silently ignored and unstructured text returned; the mcp_server_errors field needs v2.1.219 or later.
